extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental investigators, and students of inductive method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for collecting, classifying, and using special 'prerogative' instances (deviating, bordering, power, accompanying/hostile, subjunctive, alliance, cross, etc.) as part of an inductive method to discover forms and causes in natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviating instances (errors of nature / strange and monstrous objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deviating instances, such as the errors of nature, or strange and monstrous objects, in which nature deviates and turns from her ordinary course. The errors of nature differ from singular instances, inasmuch as the latter are the miracles of species, the former of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to rectify the understanding opposed to habit and to reveal common forms; inquire until the cause of the deviation is discerned (the cause may be only the latent process toward a form). They are apt for practice and the operative branch because varying known species is easier than generating new ones. Compile a particular natural history of all monsters and prodigious births, selecting rigorously so as to be worthy of credit; avoid relying on superstition, writers of natural magic or alchemy (who love fables); prefer grave and credible history and faithful narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bordering instances (participants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bordering instances (participants) exhibit species that appear composed of two species, or rudiments between one and the other; rare and extraordinary, they may be classed with singular or heteroclite instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat separately because they point out order and constitution of things and suggest causes of number and quality of common species, leading understanding from that which is to that which is possible. Examples: moss (between putrescence and plant), some comets (between stars and ignited meteors), flying fishes (between fishes and birds), bats (between birds and quadrupeds), biformed foetus, mingled species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of power (the wit or hands of man; masterpieces of art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of power are such works as are most noble and perfect — the masterpieces in every art — sometimes called the wit or hands of man (fasces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine all mechanical and practical liberal arts and compile histories of the great masterpieces and modes of effecting them. From contemplation of such works one may advance, adapt, or apply them to new purposes. Beware that masterpieces do not 'depress' or fix the understanding (i.e., make one think nothing new can be done unless the same means are used). Prefer artificial works which approach imitation of nature or powerfully govern/change her course. Do not entirely despise charms, conjuring, superstition, or magic: although overwhelmed by fables, investigate for possible latent natural operations (e.g., fascination, sympathy, transmission of impressions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the similar, singular, deviating, bordering, and power instances as a preparative collection
rubrics_metrics.description: The similar, singular, deviating and bordering instances, and those of power, should be collected at once in the style of a particular history rather than reserved for investigation of any single nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a compilation arranges matter entering the understanding and corrects its depraved habit (daily impressions corrupt the understanding). Use them as preparatives to level and purify the understanding and to prepare the way for the operative branch; they withdraw the mind from habit and ready it for true notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and credibility of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances must be selected with rigorous care and should be derived from grave and credible history and faithful narration rather than superstition or fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspect instances that depend on superstition (e.g., prodigies of Livy) or come from writers of natural magic/alchemy. Prefer well-attested, credible reports; rigorous selection is necessary for a trustworthy compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompanying and hostile instances (inseparable companion or constant avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accompanying instances exhibit a body where the required nature is constantly found as an inseparable companion; hostile instances exhibit where the required nature is constantly avoided and excluded from attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to form certain and universal propositions (affirmative or negative) about concretes and predicates. They narrow the affirmative of a form (e.g., flame always accompanies heat). Allow exceptions if singular/rare. If no universal affirmative or negative exists, note its non-existence. For universals, subjoin concretes that approach the non-existing substance to show limits (e.g., least-burning flames, gold approaching incorruptibility). Examples: flame as accompanying heat; air as hostile to solidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjunctive instances (instances of extremity or limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjunctive instances, also called instances of extremity or limits, indicate the real divisions of nature, measures of things, and 'how far' nature effects or allows anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extremes in abundance and defect to mark limits (examples: gold in weight, iron in hardness, whale in animal size, dog in smell, flame of gunpowder in rapid expansion; or spirits of wine in weight, worms on skin for smallness). They serve to delimit forms and measure degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of alliance or union
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of alliance or union are cases where natures held to be heterogeneous mingle and unite, showing that an effect considered peculiar to one may be attributed to another, proving that differences are not essential but modifications of a common nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to lift understanding from differences to genera and remove misleading 'phantoms' in concrete substances. Investigate how apparently distinct kinds of a nature differ in degree, quality, inequality, and duration (example: four differences between heat of sun and fire: degree, moisture/quality, inequality/variation, and duration/tempering). Provide experimental examples (vine branch ripened by building fire, reviving butterflies by gentle warmth, hatching eggs by fire) to show modifiability. Apply to motion, weight/gravity, discursive power of mind (animal examples), vision/light/color, etc., to show continuity between classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the cross (decisive, judicial, or oracle instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of the cross are decisive/judicial instances used when the understanding is balanced between two or more candidate natures; they show that the union of one nature with the required nature is firm while the other is separable, thereby deciding the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek or design such instances expressly to decide between hypotheses; they may be new observations or be found among existing instances. Use cross instances to reject or accept causes by showing implications that would be impossible under one hypothesis. Examples and experimental designs given: (1) tides — inquire whether flood/ebb are simultaneous on opposite coasts (Panama/Lima) to reject progressive-motion hypothesis; (2) sounding straits to detect sea curvature differences between ebb and flood to test magnetic-raising hypothesis; (3) observation of motion east-to-west in ocean, air, comets, planets to decide whether diurnal motion is in the heavens or the earth; (4) clocks driven by weights vs springs placed at height/depth to test whether attraction of earth's mass causes gravity; (5) small magnetic globe and untouched needle experiment to test whether magnet touch is necessary versus earth's polarity. The cross should be constructed so that if a particular empirical fact is discovered, one hypothesis must be rejected. Apply careful, directed inquiry and make use of geographical, mechanical, and magnetic experiments as decisive tests.
